The **Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action** (**JCPOA**; [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language"): برنامه جامع اقدام مشترک, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Persian "Romanization of Persian"): *barnāmeye jāme'e eqdāme moshtarak* (برجام, **BARJAM**)),[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) more commonly known as the **Iran nuclear deal** or **Iran deal**, was an [agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_and_culture_of_negotiation_in_Iran "History and culture of negotiation in Iran") to limit the [Iranian nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran "Nuclear program of Iran") in return for sanctions relief and other provisions. The agreement was finalized in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") on 14 July 2015, between Iran and the [P5+1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P5+1 "P5+1") (the five [permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (UNSC)—China, France, Russia, the U.K., U.S.—plus Germany)[[a]](#cite_note-9) together with the European Union.

Formal negotiations began with the adoption of the [Joint Plan of Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Plan_of_Action "Joint Plan of Action"), an interim agreement signed between Iran and the P5+1 countries in November 2013. Iran and the P5+1 countries engaged in negotiations for the following 20 months and, in April 2015, agreed on a [framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_nuclear_deal_framework "Iran nuclear deal framework"), which later led to JCPOA, along with a Roadmap Agreement between Iran and the [International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") (IAEA).[[9]](#cite_note-10)

Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to constrain its [nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran "Nuclear program of Iran") by limiting fuel cycle activities that could lead to the production of weapons-grade uranium or plutonium. The JCPOA restricted the number and type of [centrifuges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_uranium#Centrifuge_techniques "Enriched uranium") in operation, the level of [uranium enrichment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_enrichment "Uranium enrichment"), and the size of Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. Key facilities at [Fordow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordow_Uranium_Enrichment_Plant "Fordow Uranium Enrichment Plant"), [Natanz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natanz_Nuclear_Facility "Natanz Nuclear Facility") and [Arak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IR-40 "IR-40") were repurposed for civilian uses such as medical and industrial research. Iran agreed to accept more intrusive IAEA monitoring measures of its fuel-cycle related activities. In exchange for complying with these restrictions, Iran received relief from [nuclear-related sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_against_Iran "International sanctions against Iran") imposed by the United Nations, the EU, and the United States, but many U.S. sanctions unrelated to the nuclear issue—targeting Iran's missile program, support for militant groups, and human rights record—remained in place, limiting the economic effect of sanctions relief. The agreement also set a timetable to lift the UN arms embargo, contingent on Iran's continued compliance with civilian nuclear commitments.

The agreement took effect on 20 January 2016.[[10]](#cite_note-FinalDays-11) It was criticized and opposed by Israel, Saudi Arabia, [Iranian principlists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_principlists "Iranian principlists"), and the [Republican

**AUKUS** ( [*AW-kəs*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")), also styled as **Aukus**, is a trilateral security partnership between [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), which have stated that its goals are to "promote a free and open [Indo-Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") that is secure and stable."[[1]](#cite_note-:8-1) Initially announced on 15 September 2021, the partnership involves two lines of effort referred to as pillars.[[2]](#cite_note-Announce-2)[[3]](#cite_note-CRSR47599-3) Pillar 1 focuses on Australia acquiring [nuclear-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_submarine "Nuclear submarine") [attack submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_submarine "Attack submarine") and the rotational basing of US and UK nuclear-powered attack submarines in Australia.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Pillar 2 entails the collaborative development of advanced capabilities in six technological areas: undersea capabilities, [quantum technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_technology "Quantum technology"), [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") and autonomy, advanced [cyber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberwarfare "Cyberwarfare"), [hypersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_weapon "Hypersonic weapon") and [counter-hypersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_defense "Missile defense") capabilities, and [electronic warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare "Electronic warfare"); and in two broader functional areas: innovation and information sharing.[[5]](#cite_note-FactSheet-5)[[3]](#cite_note-CRSR47599-3)

AUKUS is widely seen as a response to the perception among its members that the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") poses a threat to the Indo-Pacific region.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) The Chinese government said, when the partnership was announced, that it risked "severely damaging regional peace" and had a "[cold-war mentality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Cold_War "Second Cold War")".[[8]](#cite_note-8)

A direct result of the creation of the partnership was Australia's controversial cancellation of a French-Australian [submarine contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack-class_submarine "Attack-class submarine") worth [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro")56 billion ([A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")90 billion).[[9]](#cite_note-recall-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) The Australian government only gave the French government a few hours' notice of this before the public announcement of AUKUS.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-ABC17Sep2021-12) The Australian government agreed to a €555 million ([US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")584 million) compensation settlement with French defence contractor [Naval Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Group "Naval Group").[[13]](#cite_note-CNN2022-13)[[14]](#cite_note-AJ2022-14)

### Naval Group–Australia strategic partnership agreement

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Naval Group–Australia strategic partnership agreement")]

In 2009, two years after the start of the project to replace the [Royal Australian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Australian_Navy "Royal Australian Navy")'s [conventionally-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine#Diesel%E2%80%93electric_transmission "Submarine") [*Collins*-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collins-class_submarine "Collins-class submarine") submarines, the Australian Defence White Paper stated: "The Government has ruled out nuclear propulsion for these submarines".[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In 2016, [Prime Mini

ster of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Australia "Prime Minister of Australia") [Malcolm Turnbull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Turnbull "Malcolm Turnbull") signed a A$50 billion (€31 billion) deal with the majority French government-owned company [Naval Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Group "Naval Group") (known as DCNS until 2017) to design a new generation of submarines, known as the [*Attack* class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack-class_submarine "Attack-class submarine"), under the "Future Submarine Program", scheduled to replace the *Collins* class.[[16]](#cite_note-ABC-15-sep-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[note 1]](#cite_note-21) The design was based on the latest French nuclear-powered [attack submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_submarine "Attack submarine"), the [Barracuda class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffren-class_submarine "Suffren-class submarine"), which required converting the nuclear propulsion to conventional propulsion. Another difference was that Australia chose to equip it with a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") combat system and torpedo with [Lockheed Martin Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin") selected to integrate them into the design.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report202015-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)[[23]](#cite_note-24) Australia typically requires that part of their vessels be built there, which increases the cost. In this case it corresponded to 60 per cent of the contract value, with France handling the technology transfer.[[24]](#cite_note-25)

In 2019, Australia signed a strategic partnership agreement with Naval Group to design and construct twelve submarines to be built in Australia.[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report20206,8,9-26)[[26]](#cite_note-27) However, the project was beset by delays and cost overruns, leading to uncertainty and tension behind the scenes.[[9]](#cite_note-recall-9)[[27]](#cite_note-Reuters22Sept-28) The revised cost, including inflation during the length of the program, was A$90 billion (€56 billion).[[28]](#cite_note-29)

In February 2021, an initial design plan was rejected as being too expensive, and Naval Group were given until September to improve their proposal.[[29]](#cite_note-paris-30) At a [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Australia "Senate of Australia") inquiry in early June 2021, with delays ongoing, Defence Secretary [Greg Moriarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Moriarty "Greg Moriarty") revealed under questioning that he had considered making contingency plans if the French project was to fail, admitting that there had been ongoing problems[*[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")*] for over a year.[[30]](#cite_note-31) Two weeks later, Australian prime minister [Scott Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison "Scott Morrison") met French president [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron") in Paris and expressed concern about the project going off track, to which Macron replied that France was giving "full and complete" commitment and would proceed "further and faster if possible".[[29]](#cite_note-paris-30)

On 30 August 2021, the French and Australian defence and foreign affairs ministers released a joint statement reaffirming the project, stating that the "Ministers underlined the importance of the Future Submarine program."[[31]](#cite_note-Aug30Statement-32)[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33)[[33]](#cite_note-GuardianSept18-34)

Less than three weeks later, Australia decided to publicly cancel the contract with Naval Group for the *Attack* class submarines[[16]](#cite_note-ABC-15-sep-16) despite having already spent about [A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")2.4 billion on the French project.[[34]](#cite_note-:1-35) It was expected that Australia would have to pay hundreds of millions of euros in penalties for cancelling the contract.[[35]](#cite_note-36) The contract contained "control gates" with "off-ramps" at which point Australia could withdraw from the contract.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report202028,_30-37)[[37]](#cite_note-6PR-38)

The Australian [Department of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Defence_(Australia) "Department of Defence (Australia)") wrote to Naval Group on the same day the security partnership was announced.[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33)[[38]](#cite_note-39) The French Ministry of Defence claim the department told them that "they were satisfied with the submarine's achievable performance and with the progress of the program."[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33) Naval Group said that Australia "terminated the contract for convenience".[[39]](#cite_note-40)

I have used my 6 calls. I have rich material on AUKUS (submarine nonproliferation exemption) and the JCPOA context, plus the CTBT Annex 2 list confirming U.S. has not ratified. Let me synthesize.

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 1B.4 Research Note

**Lens:** 1B.4 — Did the ruler support arms-control, inspection, nonproliferation, disarmament, or de-escalation agreements in good faith?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record is mixed-to-negative on this lens. The single most consequential action was the **March 13, 2023 AUKUS submarine deal signing in San Diego**, which established a precedent that *loosened* non-proliferation safeguards (specifically the requirement for IAEA inspections on nuclear material transferred for non-explosive military use) and was widely criticized by non-proliferation experts. Russia suspended New START on Feb 21, 2023; the administration did not retaliate by suspending in kind and kept channels open, but did not achieve reactivation. JCPOA revival talks were dormant — Iran's nuclear program advanced (60% enrichment, IAEA inspector restrictions) without an agreement. CTBT remained unratified. On the favorable side, the **Oct 30 AI EO** strengthened AI-related non-proliferation and CBRN safeguards; non-proliferation sanctions continued against Russian, Iranian, and North Korean nuclear supply chains; and the Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15) re-established a U.S.–China nuclear dialogue channel.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — AUKUS submarine deal signed Mar 13, 2023 — exemption from full-scope IAEA safeguards

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (compiling official statements, government press releases, and IAEA Board of Governors documents)
- **Date:** AUKUS announced Sep 15, 2021; "optimal pathway" announced Mar 13, 2023 at San Diego
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** AUKUS is a trilateral security partnership announced Sep 15, 2021 between Australia, the UK, and the U.S., with two pillars. Pillar 1 covers the transfer of nuclear-powered attack submarines to Australia — a class of vessel previously banned from Australian service — including the rotational basing of US/UK SSNs at Australian ports. Pillar 2 covers joint development of advanced capabilities (undersea, quantum, AI/autonomy, cyber, hypersonic, EW). On March 13, 2023, in San Diego, Biden hosted PM Rishi Sunak and PM Anthony Albanese and announced the "optimal pathway" — committing the U.S. to sell Australia three Virginia-class SSNs in the 2030s, with a new AUKUS-class SSN to follow. The deal required negotiating a bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement because conventional non-proliferation law required Australia to place all nuclear material under comprehensive IAEA safeguards — an exemption from full-scope safeguards for nuclear propulsion material (an arrangement historically granted only to the U.S., UK, France, Russia, China). Antony Blinken and Lloyd Austin said Australia had "no reciprocal requirements" such as hosting U.S. intermediate-range missiles. China called the deal a Cold-War provocation and a non-proliferation setback.
- **Direct question ID:** 1B.4 (working against 1B.4 — loosens non-proliferation safeguards; opens a pathway for additional states to seek similar exemptions; criticized by IAEA ex-officials and non-proliferation NGOs like ICAN and ACA)

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 1B.4

- **AUKUS submarine deal.** The single most consequential 2023 non-proliferation event in which Biden participated. The bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement that allows Australia to possess nuclear-propulsion material without full-scope safeguards is a precedent. Critics: former IAEA Director Mohamed ElBaradei called the deal "a serious blow to the non-proliferation regime"; ACA's Kelsey Davenport and ICAN similarly criticized the precedent; the Non-Aligned Movement and China formally objected. Proponents (U.S., UK, Australia, France) argued the deal strengthens deterrence against China without weakening non-proliferation.
- **JCPOA failure to revive.** Biden's 2020 campaign promise to rejoin JCPOA was unfulfilled. Iran's nuclear program advanced with reduced IAEA access — the 2023 IAEA Director General reports documented 60% enrichment, ~30 kg of 60% enriched uranium, and reduced inspector presence.
- **No CTBT ratification.** Failure to push Senate ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty in 2023 left the global test-moratorium regime on voluntary U.S. presidential-decision status.
- **New START collapse.** No new strategic-arms treaty framework; the Feb 21, 2023 Russian suspension ended on-site inspections. The treaty ultimately expired Feb 5, 2026 with no replacement.
- **Cluster munitions transfer.** Bypassed the global norm against area-effect munitions.
- **Modernization lock-in.** Sentinel, B61-12, W93, Columbia-class, B-21 programs continue — critics argue this forecloses future arms-control deals.

## Favorable evidence on 1B.4

- **Restraint in New START response.** Did not retaliate by suspending U.S. participation; kept strategic-stability dialogue channel open.
- **AI EO non-proliferation safeguards.** Concrete institutional non-proliferation/dual-use safeguards in AI domain.
- **AUKUS was a legal arrangement.** Conducted with IAEA cooperation and within NPT boundaries — the State Department and IAEA published an article-by-article arrangement in 2024.
- **Bilateral nuclear dialogue with China reactivated.** Biden–Xi APEC meeting re-established mil-to-mil communications, a key arms-control-adjacent channel.
- **Continued sanctions enforcement.** Russian, Iranian, North Korean nuclear-related entities remained under OFAC/BIS sanctions.
- **No nuclear test.** Continued 1992 moratorium on U.S. nuclear testing; no public advocacy of resumption.
- **Ukraine cluster munitions framed as risk-reduction.** Public justification centered on avoiding Russian battlefield gains that would escalate NATO–Russia direct conflict.
